thesis.headline: The market is pricing a Fed hike into a CPI print, with Brent through $100 and the Treasury actively fighting the long end.
thesis.body: Four things are colliding inside six sessions. Warsh's Jackson Hole speech moved September from a hold to a coin-flip-plus on a 25bp hike. August payrolls tripled consensus. Brent cleared $100 for the first time since May on the Iran conflict. And the 10-year sits at its highest since October 2023 even as Treasury doubles long-end buybacks to hold it down. The tell to watch is not the level of any one of these but the fact that the Treasury and the Fed are now pulling in opposite directions on the same part of the curve.
thesis.positioning_note: Vol is not paid for this. VIX at 15.7 into a CPI print and an FOMC that is genuinely two-sided is the cheapest thing on the screen.

modules.label: FOMC, 15–16 September
reasons: Genuinely two-sided for the first time in this cycle — the market is pricing a hike, not a cut
Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks moved implied odds from ~36% to the high 50s inside a session
modules.detail: Market-implied probability of a 25bp hike has run 36% → 56% → 60.4% → 57% since 28 August. A hike would be the first of the cycle's second leg and would land against a Treasury that is publicly trying to cap long yields. The July meeting already carried three dissents against the hold, so the committee is not unified.

modules.label: August CPI — tomorrow, 08:30 ET
reasons: Last read the committee sees before it decides
Consensus has headline holding at 3.4% y/y with core at 2.5% — both still above target
modules.detail: Warsh's stated objection is that the softer inflation run has not yet shown a meaningful improvement in the underlying trend. A core print at or above 0.3% m/m makes that argument for him and puts the hike near certain; a 0.1% would be the first real evidence against it. Energy is the wildcard — Brent has gone from the mid-90s to $101 inside the sample window, though the pass-through lands mostly in the September and October prints, not this one.
modules.caveat: Consensus figures vary by survey — Kiplinger and Babypips carried different headline m/m estimates (+0.4% vs +0.2%). Treat the range, not the point.

modules.label: Treasury and the Fed are now pulling opposite ways
reasons: Treasury doubled long-end buybacks to $4bn effective 9 September, the same week the Fed is being priced to hike
This is the structural story behind the long end, and it is not a one-meeting event
modules.detail: Bessent has raised the maximum long-end liquidity-support buyback from $2bn to at least $4bn per operation in the 10–20y and 20–30y sectors, effective 9 September and running through the 4 November refunding. The stated rationale is liquidity support. The market reads it as an attempt to cap term premium. Meanwhile Warsh is signalling tighter policy. One arm of the government is buying duration while the other is repricing it lower. That tension is why the 10-year can sit at cycle highs while official buying steps up, and it is the single most important thing on this page for anyone running duration risk.
watch: Whether buyback operations start clearing at levels that suggest price support rather than liquidity provision
The 4 November refunding for whether coupon sizes or bill share change
Any public friction between Treasury and the Fed — Axios has already framed them as at odds

modules.label: 10-year at 4.85%
reasons: Highest since October 2023
Long end leading — this is term premium and supply, not a front-end repricing
modules.detail: The move is concentrated in the long end. 2s10s is positive but narrow, so the curve is bear-flattening from the back: the market is adding term premium for oil-driven inflation and a fiscal path running above $2tn, while the front end is capped by an FOMC that has not yet moved. If the Fed hikes on the 16th and the long end does not follow, that flattening accelerates.

modules.label: Brent through $100
reasons: First print above $100 since May
Supply-side, not demand-side — this is the inflation input the Fed cannot look through
modules.detail: Brent reached roughly $100.76 on 9 September and cleared $101.50 on the 10th; WTI is around $94. The driver is the Iran conflict: reported Iranian attacks on US Navy vessels, and Houthi strikes on Saudi energy facilities that forced temporary shut-ins. Goldman lifted December Brent to $85 but warned of $120+ in 2027 if Gulf output stays 4mb/d below pre-war levels. A supply shock is the worst possible input for a central bank already being pushed to hike — it lifts headline inflation while cutting real income.

modules.label: Copper/gold has decoupled from the 10-year
reasons: Ratio implies a 10-year far below 4.85% — the widest gap of the cycle
But the divergence is a denominator story, not a growth warning
modules.detail: Copper at $6.76/lb over gold at $4,400/oz puts the ratio at 1.54 (×1000). Historically that tracks the 10-year reasonably closely; today the 10-year is at 4.85%. The naive read is that yields are far too high for the growth signal. That read is wrong here. Copper is up 46.6% year-on-year — the growth leg is strong. The gap exists because gold has run harder, and gold is running on a fiscal bid: a deficit tracking above $2tn, rising interest expense, and central bank accumulation. So the ratio is not signalling weak growth. It is signalling debasement, which argues for *higher* long yields, not lower. This is the clearest example on the page of a classic indicator that inverts its meaning when you check which leg actually moved.

modules.label: August payrolls tripled consensus
reasons: +162k against a +53k consensus, with June and July both revised up
Removes the labour-market argument against hiking
modules.detail: The single largest surprise in the current run. June was revised up 11k to +31k and July from −23k to +21k, a 55k two-month revision that turns a stalling labour market back into a slowly growing one. Unemployment held at 4.1%, in line. Leisure and hospitality added 62k; information and financial activities declined. For the Fed's purposes this closes off the softest branch of the dovish case — it is now an inflation argument alone.

modules.label: Deficit on a $2tn+ pace
reasons: $1.8tn borrowed in the first ten months of FY2026
Interest expense is now one of the two things driving the spending increase
modules.detail: Through ten months the deficit stands at $1.8tn and the year is tracking above $2tn. Receipts are up $143bn on stronger individual and payroll collections plus larger customs duties; outlays are up $172bn on entitlements and debt service. Debt stood at $31.7tn at end-June, $2.7tn higher than a year earlier. The feedback loop is the point: higher yields raise interest expense, which widens the deficit, which raises issuance, which pressures term premium. That loop is precisely what Treasury's buyback expansion is trying to interrupt.

modules.label: USD/JPY around 160 into a BoJ meeting
reasons: Cleared 160 on 28 August — the level that has historically drawn intervention
BoJ meets in September with the market pricing some chance of a move
modules.detail: The pair briefly cleared 160 before easing to 159.7–159.9. The tension: Japan's Q2 was weak — consumption −0.1%, capex down for the third quarter in four — and core inflation has not printed above target all year, which argues against BoJ urgency. But a Fed hike would widen differentials further and push the pair through 160 with force. Watch for verbal intervention before the meeting rather than after.

modules.label: The hiking cycle is going global
reasons: The ECB returned to hiking in June 2026 and has kept going
A synchronised tightening turn is a different regime from a US-only one
modules.detail: The ECB resumed rate increases in June and continues to tighten; the Fed is now being priced to follow; the BoJ is at least in play. A synchronised turn removes the cross-currency cushion that made the last US-only tightening tolerable for risk assets — there is no obvious easing central bank to offset. It also compresses the rate-differential trade that has driven FX all year, which is why EUR/USD has held a 1.14–1.21 range despite a hawkish Fed repricing.

modules.label: Vol is not priced for any of this
reasons: VIX at 15.7 into a CPI print and a live FOMC
The 2026 low of 14.2 was set less than a month ago
modules.detail: The S&P is around 7,636 having been up roughly 16% year-to-date at the August highs, and the VIX printed its 2026 low of 14.2 in mid-August. It has since risen — up 5.5% on 9 September as yields climbed — but 15.7 into a genuinely two-sided FOMC and a CPI release the following morning is the cheapest risk on the screen. Equity index vol is not the only expression: with the Fed and Treasury in opposite corners, rate vol is the more direct trade.
